newsitem.title: BELARUS: World Bank criticises slow reforms in Belarus.
newsitem.headline: World Bank criticises slow reforms in Belarus.

text.p: Belarus has the least liberalised economy in Europe and a fifth of its population lives below the poverty line, the World Bank said on Friday.
Christopher Willoughby, the Bank's representative in Belarus, told a news conference that the former Soviet republic was one of the most backward in terms of private sector output.
"We still hope that the government will take important steps, agreed with the World Bank, to renew measures to attract credits. But so far there has been no change," he said.
In February the World Bank and the Belarus government agreed that credits for new programmes could be renewed if a new memorandum of understanding is signed.
The bank, which has so far lent $170 million to Belarus, is prepared to issue a credit of $40 million to support private business with increases to follow.
The bank has said that if the government accepts its conditions and carries out liberalisation, annual credits could reach up to $100 million.

Willoughby said he would meet officials later on Friday to try to finalise details of the memorandum, but added: "Belarus' problem is not in the signing of documents but in their implementation. From a commercial point of view, the bank should be very careful."
The Belarus government says the state sector accounts for 90 percent of the economy.

"In the field of liberalisation Belarus is the most backward except for Azerbaijan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan," Willoughby said, explaining that by liberalisation he meant a market economy, open foreign trade, free prices and a freely convertable currency.
"According to our fairly extensive research, in Belarus 20-22 percent of the population lives below the poverty line, as defined by the minimum consumer budget," he said.
"It's a very important problem for Belarus, which is impossible to resolve with today's measures," said Willoughby.
He said subsidies and limits on the prices of bread and other basic foodstuffs and services distorted the demands of the market, put off entrepreneurs and did not protect the poor.
"These subsidies are received by the 80 percent of the population, who are not below the poverty line," he said.

According to official statistics, the average wage in Belarus in February 1997 was 1,693,600 Belarussian roubles with a minimum consumer budget at 1,405,300 roubles. The Belarussian currency now trades on the street at about 25,000 roubles to the U.S. dollar.
From April 1, the minimum wage was increased to 150,000 Belarussian roubles from 130,000.
